Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on Surah 108, verses 1–3:

Meccan, and its verses number 3. "It was revealed after Surah al-'Adiyat."

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the recitation (*qira'a*, a transmitted mode of reading) of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Inna a'taynaka" (*Indeed We have given you*), with the nun.[[Narrated by al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni in *al-Mu'talif*, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tha'labi, through the transmission of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd from al-Hasan from his mother from Umm Salama. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd is a weak narrator of hadith.]]

In his (ﷺ) hadith: "wa-anti'u al-thabija" (*and cut off the thabija*).[[This is in the hadith mentioned earlier in the commentary on Surah Yunus.]][[The words "wa-anti'u al-thabija" are explained in the *Qamus*: "al-Shabija," with a vowelled *fatha* on the first letter, refers to what is intermediate between the best and the worst. (Editor's note: 'Ayn.)]]

*Al-Kawthar* is of the form *fawʿal*, derived from *kathra* (abundance), and denotes one who is excessively abundant. It was said to an Arab woman when her son returned from a journey: "With what has your son returned?" She said: "He returned with *kawthar*." And the poet said:

*And you are abundant, O son of Marwan, good,*
*And your father was the son of noble women, a *kawthar*.*[[By al-Kumayt. "And you are abundant" means abundant in goodness and piety. In another version, "kawthar" appears in place of "abundant." In the verse there is an affirmation of his name and an exaltation of his rank. He used "good" (*tayyib*) as a metaphor for good conduct. It may also mean the opposite of "wicked" (*khabith*). "Al-'aqa'il" are the choicest women, and what is meant is their kind, or what includes the grandmothers. And *kawthar* is the intensive form in the sense of the utmost in goodness.]]

It was also said that *al-Kawthar* is a river in Paradise. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited it when it was revealed to him, and then said:

"Do you know what al-Kawthar is? It is a river in Paradise which my Lord promised me, and in it is much good."[[Narrated by Muslim through the transmission of al-Mukhtar ibn Falful from Anas, within a hadith mentioned at the beginning of the chapter on prayer.]]

And it was narrated describing it:

It is sweeter than honey, whiter than milk, colder than ice, softer than butter; its two banks are of chrysolite, and its vessels are of silver, as many as the stars of the sky.[[Narrated by al-Hakim from a hadith of Abu Barza, raised to the Prophet: "My Basin extends from Ayla to San'a: its width is like its length. In it are two spouts that pour from Paradise, sweeter than honey, colder than ice, whiter than milk, and softer than butter. In it are vessels as many as the stars of the sky…" And in Ibn Mardawayh, from a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas concerning the Night Journey, he mentioned a very long hadith, in which al-Kawthar is mentioned and its two banks are of chrysolite.]]

And it was narrated: "Whoever drinks from it will never thirst again. The first to arrive at it are the poor emigrants (*fuqara' al-muhajirin*), those with dirty clothes and disheveled hair, who do not marry women of luxury, and for whom the gates of closed doors are not opened. One of them dies while his need stirs in his breast, but if he swears by God, God will fulfil it for him."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah, Ahmad and al-Tabarani from a hadith of Thawban. In it: "My Basin extends from 'Adan to Ayla, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey; its cups are as many as the stars of the sky. Whoever drinks from it a single draught will never thirst after it again. The first to enter upon it are the poor emigrants, with dirty clothes and disheveled heads, who do not marry women of luxury, and for whom the doors are not opened."]]

And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he interpreted *al-Kawthar* as "abundant good." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said to him: "People say it is a river in Paradise!" He replied: "It is (a part) of the abundant good."

*Al-Nahr* (*sacrifice*) means the slaughter of camels. It is related from 'Ata': it is the dawn prayer at Muzdalifa, and *al-nahr* is at Mina. It was also said: it is the 'Id prayer and the sacrifice. It was also said: it is prayer in general. *Al-Nahr* also means placing the right hand upon the left (in prayer).

The meaning is: "We have given you an immeasurable abundance of the good of the two abodes (this world and the Hereafter), which no one else has been given. The giver of all this is I, the Lord of the worlds. Thus two felicities have been combined for you."[[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "That is, We have combined for you the two felicities: one of them is attaining the most noble gift, which is al-Kawthar… etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: al-Zamakhshari made the placement of the pronoun between the two parts restrictive, because its function here is clearly for that purpose.]] These are: attaining the noblest and most abundant gift, from the most generous giver and the greatest benefactor. So worship your Lord, who has honored you by giving it, exalted you, and protected you from the favors of the creatures, opposing your people who worship other than God. And sacrifice for His sake and in His name when you slaughter, differing from them in sacrificing to idols.

Indeed, whoever hates you among your people, out of opposition to you, is *al-abtar* (*the one cut off*), not you. For every believer who will be born until the Day of Resurrection is your offspring and your descendants. Your remembrance is raised upon the pulpits and the minarets, and on the tongue of every scholar and remembrer until the end of time. He begins with the remembrance of God and follows it with your remembrance. And in the Hereafter you have what cannot be described. So one like you is not called *abtar*. Rather, the *abtar* is your hater, who is forgotten in this world and the Hereafter, even if he is remembered, he is remembered with curse.

They used to say: "Muhammad is *sanbur*" (*a cut-off stump*):[[The words "innama Muhammadan sanbur" are explained in the *Qamus* as: a lone, weak, humiliated man, without family, descendants or helper. (Editor's note: 'Ayn.)]] when he dies, his remembrance dies. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il, whom they called *al-abtar*. *Al-abtar* is the one without descendants. From it comes the saying:

"The donkey is *abtar*, which has no tail."

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Kawthar, God will give him to drink from every river in Paradise, and he will be credited with ten good deeds for every sacrifice that the servants have offered on the Day of Sacrifice, or will offer."[[Narrated by al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh with their chains to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]
